name: Red light at night

image.caption: Light art, Light beams, Red Square at night, Moscow, Russia

lead: This habit replaces white household lights with red or dim red bulbs in the evening. The goal is easier sleep onset and a more rested appearance by keeping melatonin and the body clock undisturbed.

The circadian system responds most to short-wavelength (blue) light, so long-wavelength red light is proposed to interfere less. Lab findings are mixed: rat experiments found bright red light could still suppress melatonin, a horse study reported a nighttime melatonin rise under red light, and a review of light at night for shift workers noted long-wavelength light can raise alertness. No human trial has tested the habit.

paras: People install red bulbs or night lights in bedrooms, bathrooms and living areas for the last hours before bed, usually together with dimming screens and other wind-down habits.
No direct risks are documented. The effect on sleep in people has not been studied, and brighter red light may still be alerting.

web.title: Light effects on circadian rhythm - Wikipedia

angle.text: Sleep-focused communities swap white evening bulbs for red ones to keep melatonin and the body clock undisturbed, aiming for easier sleep and a more rested look. The idea follows from light science on wavelength and melatonin.

lead: Using red or dim red bulbs instead of white light in the evening is a lighting habit in sleep-focused communities, based on the idea that long-wavelength light disturbs melatonin and the body clock less than white or blue light.

Reference sources describe short-wavelength (blue) light as having the strongest effect on melatonin suppression and circadian timing.[1] Studies on red light itself are few and not specific to this habit: some animal experiments found that bright red light suppressed melatonin in rats,[2][3] while a study in horses reported that red light allowed a nighttime melatonin rise,[4] and a review of light at night for shift workers noted that long-wavelength light can raise alertness.[5]

paras: Practitioners swap white household lighting for red or dim red lamps in the hours before bed. The motivation is to keep light exposure from interfering with melatonin and sleep onset.

sections.h: Background on light and the body clock
paras: The circadian system is most sensitive to light near 480 nm, and light in the evening delays the body clock, while evening and night light can suppress melatonin.[1] Smartphones, tablets and LED lighting are described as significant sources of nighttime blue light that can delay sleep onset and reduce sleep quality.[1]

No studies found of red evening lighting for sleep or appearance outcomes in healthy people. Related laboratory research is limited: in albino rats, high-intensity red light suppressed pineal enzyme activity and melatonin about as much as white light, while low intensities produced smaller reductions.[2][3] A veterinary study in horses reported that red light at night permitted the nocturnal melatonin rise,[4] and a 2025 study examined lighting and sleep behaviour in riding-school horses.[6] A review on shift workers noted that light at night can increase alertness while also suppressing melatonin.[5]

The practice is discussed alongside screen limits and fixed sleep times as part of improving sleep for skin, recovery and energy. Evidence is mostly indirect and no source examines it for facial appearance.
